newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN OIL PRODUCTS SALES UP JUST 1.3 PCT IN Q1.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN OIL PRODUCTS SALES UP JUST 1.3 PCT IN Q1.

text.p: Sales of major petroleum products in South Africa grew only 1.3 percent in the first quarter of 1997 to 4.88 billion litres compared to 4.81 billion litres in the same period in 1996.

The South African Petroleum Industry Association (Sapia) said on Thursday that after expanding by more than six percent in the first three quarters of last year, sales growth slowed down to 4.9 percent in the last quarter.
"The association then said that it was too early to interpret the lower growth as a slowdown in the demand for petroleum products," Sapia said.
"The slowdown has, however, continued and intensified in the first quarter of 1997.

"This decline in growth of sales volumes will have a material adverse impact on the industry, which has been operating on fixed cents a litre marketing margins, unchanged since September 1993, despite an increase in the CPI of over 33 percent since tht date."
The industry has asked for a three cents a litre margin increase but government has stalled on a decision.

Gasoline sales, which account for more than half of total sales, fell by 0.4 percent to 2.60 billion litres from 2.61 billion litres while diesel sales rose 1.3 percent to 1.33 billion litres from 1.31 billion litres.
Jet fuel sales resisted the trend to slower growth and grew by 22.5 percent to 425 million litres from 347 million litres.
Sales of illuminating paraffin, on which many South Africans depend for cooking, heating, lighting and refrigeration, fell by 3.9 percent to 195 million litres from 206 million litres.
Fuel oil sales fell 3.7 percent to 158 million litres from 164 million litres.
Bitumen sales fell 13.1 percent to 53 million litres from 61 million litres and liquified petroleum gas sales rose 1.8 percent to 112 million litres from 110 million litres.
Sapia said that unleaded gasoline, introduced last year, now accounted for 9.5 percent of petrol sales.
